thoughts: At the end of a German word, g is usually devoiced. The separate ending -ig has its own guide.
description: Pronounce final g like the k in English “back,” not like the g in “bag.”

thoughts: A single s at the end of a German word is voiceless, even when it follows a vowel. Avoid examples ending in ss, ß, or longer guided combinations such as chs.
description: Pronounce final s like the s in English “ice,” not the z sound in “is.”

thoughts: A final single e is usually an unstressed schwa. These examples avoid endings such as -en and -er, which have their own guides.
description: At the end of a word, e usually sounds like the short, unstressed “uh” in English “sofa.” Keep it light; don’t pronounce it as “ee.”

thoughts: At the end of a German word, unstressed -en usually has a very weak e; the n may form a syllable on its own.
description: Say a light “uh-n,” or let the n carry the syllable: Garten sounds roughly like “GAR-tn.” Avoid a clear “en” as in English “hen.”

thoughts: At the end of an unstressed syllable, er is usually a single vowel sound; the r is not pronounced like an English r.
description: Unstressed final er sounds roughly like a relaxed “uh,” with no distinct English-style r. For example, Wasser sounds approximately like “VAH-suh.”

thoughts: At the end of a German word, unstressed -el usually has a very weak vowel before the l; the vowel may be barely audible.
description: Say a light “uh-l,” often with the “uh” barely audible. It is similar to the ending of English “little.” Do not pronounce it like “ell.”

thoughts: Word-final r after a vowel is usually vocalized in standard German. These examples avoid the separate -er ending.
description: At the end of a word, r after a vowel usually sounds like a brief, relaxed “uh” glide. In Bier, for example, let the vowel trail off rather than pronouncing a strong English r.
